analysis.one_liner: Lets low-income housing tax credit owners extend affordability rules for extra tax credits.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never got a committee hearing, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Affordable apartments built with the low-income housing tax credit only have to stay affordable for 15 years; after that, owners can raise rents or sell at market rates. This bill would let owners voluntarily extend those rent restrictions for 30 or 50 years and, in exchange, receive a fresh round of tax credits. It also would lift the state volume cap on private activity bonds used to refinance these buildings during the extended period.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters in tax-credit apartments whose rent restrictions are set to expire, because their units would stay under affordable-rent rules longer. Owners and investors of those buildings also gain, since they would receive additional tax credits for extending the affordability period.

how_it_helps.text: Lets a taxpayer elect to extend a building's compliance period to 30 or 50 years, replacing the standard 15-year affordability window, in exchange for a new 15-year credit period [S2].
Excludes bonds used to refinance these extended affordable buildings from the state private activity bond volume cap, making refinancing easier during the longer compliance period [S2].
Directs state allocating agencies to give preference to projects that make this extension election when distributing credits [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost of the additional tax credits claimed by owners who extend their affordability periods. Owners who do not elect the extension face no new obligations.

drawbacks.text: The extension is voluntary, so owners would take the extra credits only where the numbers work for them, meaning federal revenue is spent building on deals investors already favored [S2].
Extending affordability for a building costs the Treasury another round of credits rather than funding new affordable units, so existing tenants benefit at the expense of building anything new.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is straightforward: longer affordability for existing units in exchange for more tax credits to owners. It is a reasonable design for preserving housing that would otherwise convert to market rents, but it is voluntary, so taxpayers pay extra credits only on deals owners choose, and the credits subsidize existing buildings rather than new construction.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Wiley Nickel introduced the bill on June 28, 2024, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S4].
The Ways and Means Committee took no further action, and the bill received no floor vote before the Congress ended [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: owners of expiring tax-credit buildings received no extra credits and the Treasury kept the revenue, while renters got no extension of affordability either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury, and the status quo

for.name: Rep. Wiley Nickel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it at introduction; it was referred to Ways and Means.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, never held a markup or vote, and let it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No other member of either party cosponsored the bill, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition shows up in the record [S3].

industries.industry: Low-income housing tax credit investors and syndicators
industries.note: Owners of expiring affordable buildings would receive a new round of tax credits for extending rent restrictions, a direct gain, but only in exchange for keeping units affordable longer. In this bill the industry's interest and renters' interest run together.

industries.industry: Municipal bond issuers and housing finance agencies
industries.note: Refinancing bonds for extended buildings would bypass the state private activity bond volume cap, and state agencies would favor these projects in credit allocations.
